item.title: The Hidden Cost of Resting on Your Laurels
item.description:
Motivation

The Hidden Cost of Resting on Your Laurels

Why your last big win might be quietly stalling your next one.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Big wins are empowering, but they can breed complacency.
  • Momentum creates a self-reinforcing loop.
  • Small, effort-based wins sustain momentum better than big, outcome-based ones.

Being a published author had always been important to Alex. It was a solid item on his dream board for years. He would envision what the book looked like, a sophisticated, attractive cover, an inviting title, and a subtitle that promised real results. He imagined what it would feel like to see his book on the shelves at the local bookstore, and how awesome it would be to sign books and interact with readers after a Q&A session. And it wasn’t a vanity project either. Writing was something that brought him a lot of joy. Immersing deep in the world of ideas, explaining complex research and concepts for practical application, and using words — the way an artist uses colors to paint new images — to bring to life new ideas and inspiration.

You can imagine the excitement when his first book was published! It was everything he expected and more! After an intense couple of years of researching, writing, editing, proofing, in repeated loops, his efforts had paid off. It was time to rest and take it all in.

He promised himself that he would start working on the sequel soon. He had a few ideas about what to write next. But not yet. He needed to enjoy the fruits of his labor a little longer. He was in a good place. He had proof he could manage writing a book. He stopped questioning his ability. Any symptoms of impostor syndrome he had before the book went public went away. What also went away was his momentum. His writing became sporadic. His research was erratic. His ideas started multiplying and overwhelming him. He continued to reassure himself that he got this, he’ll pick up when he’s ready.

Life after the big win

As time went on, Alex was stalled. No new book, not even a solid outline. He started wondering whether his first book would be his only book. He’d be the one-hit wonder, assuming the first and only book was even a hit, which Alex started doubting. As more years went by, the impostor feelings returned. His confidence eroded. He wasn’t sure he had what it took to write anything worthwhile. None of his ideas seemed novel or inspiring anymore. It’s all been said and done before. Alex had lost his momentum.

Psychological momentum is an internal power-generator that boosts a person’s beliefs about their efficacy, competence, and probability of future success. Often referred to as the success-breeds-success principle, it is an important component of what sustains effort in the pursuit of a challenging goal. You can read more about momentum and the research that supports it in my post Why Momentum Matters More than Motivation.

Alex did what most of us do after a big win that takes everything we’ve got. He rested on his laurels. He stopped writing as often, and what he wrote he kept mostly to himself. He wasn’t putting much content out there. He wasn’t testing new ideas and wasn’t getting any feedback from followers. Resting on his laurels way too long undercut his momentum. And without momentum, he became complacent.

Complacency isn’t laziness or overconfidence. It is a false sense of security and comfort that’s supported by the belief that if you’ve been successful in the past, you’ll continue to be successful in the future. So, you can rest on your laurels, assured that future success is guaranteed. Complacency isn’t unique to authors, like Alex. It applies to many different situations and life goals. Someone who’s at risk of being laid off may think: “I’ve been able to find a job easily in the past, it will be easy to find another job in the future.” Someone who gained an uncomfortable amount of weight may say, “I’ve lost weight before, I can lose it again when I’m ready.” Perhaps Alex was thinking, “I had a book published, I’m sure I can have another one published.”

But here’s the glitch. Momentum relies on a self-reinforcing loop of effort and progress: you work towards a goal, you see progress, you feel confident and optimistic, you keep working toward the goal, you make more progress, and so on. But after a big win — after unexpectedly making a lot of progress — people ease up on effort. Research shows that such big wins could make a person reduce effort on the goal at hand and drift toward other goals. The momentum loop stalls. When you ease up effort, you slow down progress, and you lose momentum. After his big win of publishing a book, Alex rested on his laurels longer than was necessary to keep the momentum going. The big win faded into the past and wasn’t powerful enough to keep his engine going.

Reigniting momentum

So, what can you do to keep the momentum going, even after a big win?

  • Celebrate the big wins. They are well-deserved products of your efforts. Accept the laurel, frame it, show it off. Celebrating the big win doesn’t translate into complacency. It implies acknowledgment. The idea behind the resting-on-laurels effect is not to minimize your accomplishments. It is to use them as springboards and to be mindful that they don’t become traps.
  • Design small wins. Small wins are low-effort milestones toward a bigger goal. My suggestion is to create wins that are effort-based instead of outcome-based. Defining “wins” as doing the work protects you from linking your self-efficacy to uncontrollable factors that determine outcomes. For example, if landing a stimulating job is your goal, small wins could include doing specific job searches, completing applications, or targeted networking. If losing weight is the goal, small wins could be skipping dessert or picking up your pace during a walk for exercise. You may wonder, are effort-based wins real victories? They may not feel like victories in the moment, but they are proof that you’re playing the long game.
  • Develop consistency. I’m sure this is not the first time you've heard about this, but the importance of consistency in building routines and habits that promote progress toward a goal cannot be overstated. Whatever actions you identified as important steps to move closer to a goal, turn them into planned activities. You may have also heard that building a consistent habit takes 30 days or 400 hours or something like that, but the truth is that consistency can take a single second. The moment you make a firm decision to commit to small wins, the wheels begin to turn, and planning and execution will flow easily. If Alex had been writing one page a week, after his book was published, he would have 520 pages of material after his decade of resting on his laurels.

Alex's book is still the only one on his shelf for now. But complacency isn't a life sentence. The moment he starts writing his one page a week, the sequel stops being a someday idea and starts becoming a new big win.

item.title: 2 Signs Your Partner Is Built For Long-Term Partnership
item.description:
Relationships

2 Signs Your Partner Is Built For Long-Term Partnership

Here are research-backed ways to test your mettle as partners.

Posted June 30, 2026

Source: Everton Vila / Unsplash

When we start falling for someone, our immediate thoughts aren’t always practical. For many, love begins as a whirlwind period where infatuation, chemistry and excitement eclipse nearly everything else. We focus on how deeply we feel for our partner, and not necessarily on whether our relationship with them can actually withstand the realities of life.

But in the grand scheme of adulthood, durability is what ultimately reigns. Most people imagine a future where they’ve built some kind of stability. And if you hope to one day settle down with someone who will treat you with the same care and commitment you offer them, passion alone isn’t enough to guarantee that future.

Here are two of the clearest signs your partner is long-term material.

1. Your Partner Shares Your Goals and Values

A partner who has the same goals and values as you is every bit as attractive as someone who’s successful, charming or physically appealing — if not more so. That’s because deep compatibility instills a sense of emotional security that things like passion and chemistry simply can’t.

Surface-level similarities (e.g., liking the same music, hobbies, TV shows, etc.) can absolutely be beneficial. But they can only take a relationship so far. For the vast majority of couples, longevity is determined by whether or not they agree on the major structural questions of life: children, finances, religion, caregiving roles, career priorities, where to live and what kind of future they ultimately want.

When two people are aligned on these bigger-picture issues, compromise becomes far easier. Sacrifices don’t feel as painful because both people are ultimately moving toward the same destination. But when their core goals are fundamentally at odds, they’ll regularly find themselves feeling dissatisfied or having arguments that can’t ever be resolved.

In a 2023 study published in Personality and Individual Differences, researchers found that certain forms of personality and value similarity were associated with greater relationship satisfaction among dating couples. Specifically, traits linked to emotional stability, conscientiousness and agreeableness — as well as shared “self-transcendence” values like care, compassion and concern for others — were the most consistent predictors of satisfaction.

In other words, compatibility is a matter of whether or not your way of approaching life fundamentally fits together with your partner’s.

Imagine a relationship in which both partners are set on having geographic stability, maintaining close family ties and raising their children in one place. When career opportunities arise, their discussions may still be difficult, but their overall alignment makes compromise feel worth it in the end. Their decisions feel collaborative rather than adversarial.

Now compare that to a couple where one partner dreams of a life of travelling and adventure, while the other desperately wants rootedness and proximity to family. Neither person is necessarily wrong, but their relationship together would be a constant negotiation between two incompatible futures — worse, neither has a chance to end up truly happy if they stay together.

The most helpful approach is paying attention to four areas in particular:

  • Your vision for the future (e.g., marriage, relocation, having kids, etc.)
  • Your deal-breakers (e.g., political, spiritual, social, family-related, etc.)
  • Your money priorities (e.g., expectations for saving, spending, etc.)
  • Your caregiving expectations (e.g., kids, each other, aging relatives, etc.)

A healthy long-term relationship can only be achieved between two partners who have compatible trajectories. They don’t need to be identical, but they need to be possible without one eclipsing the other.

2. Your Partner Accepts Your Repair Attempts

No matter how compatible two people are, conflict is inevitable. The real question is whether the relationship knows how to recover from it. This is why renowned relationship researcher Dr. John Gottman argues that one of the strongest indicators of long-term relationship stability is “repair acceptance”: a partner’s willingness to accept attempts to de-escalate conflict, as opposed to continually attacking, withdrawing or trying to “win” the fight.

These repair attempts are usually modest, but they still play an integral role in whether conflict leads to positive change. They include things like:

  • “I’m sorry. Let me try saying that differently.”
  • “Okay, we’re getting heated. Can we pause?”
  • Reaching for your partner’s hand during an argument
  • Cracking gentle humor to reduce tension
  • Saying, “I understand why you’re upset.”
  • Following up later after cooling down

Gottman’s 2015 study, published in the Journal of Family Psychotherapy, found that effective repair attempts were pivotal in reducing negative emotion and restoring positive emotional connection during conflict.

Interestingly, he found that the most effective repairs were usually emotional rather than logical. This meant that tools like shared humor, affection, empathy, taking partial responsibility and reassuring statements like “we’re okay” were the most powerful in helping couples reconnect. Notably, he also found that “pre-emptive” repairs (i.e., attempts made early in conflict before escalation fully takes hold) were particularly effective.

When conflict persistently goes unresolved in a relationship, it starts tainting moments outside of the conflict itself, too. One partner is always apologizing and extending olive branches; the other gives the cold shoulder or acts bitter until they’re “over it.” When this becomes the norm after every conflict, disagreements start to feel like a legitimate threat to your livelihood.

If your partner is adept at initiating or accepting repair attempts, then arguments tend to end with statements like:

  • “Okay, let’s start over.”
  • “I hear you.”
  • “I’m still upset, but I don’t want us fighting like this.”
  • “Let’s talk later when we’ve both calmed down.”

Contrastingly, rejected repairs look or sound more like:

  • Sarcasm
  • Eye-rolling
  • Escalating criticism
  • Silent treatment
  • Mocking apologies
  • Refusing to engage

To gauge whether or not your partner embodies this trait, pay attention the next time you and they have a mild disagreement. Try offering a small repair (e.g., soften your tone, apologize, ask to pause, attempt humor, etc.) and observe whether your partner accepts it or punishes it. In a truly healthy relationship, de-escalation is a mandatory part of conflict because both partners recognize the importance of maintaining a safe baseline.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: The Silent Struggle of Student-Athletes
item.description:
Sport and Competition

The Silent Struggle of Student-Athletes

Why strength, identity, and stigma keep athletes from seeking help.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Student-athletes face psychological barriers to seeking mental health support that go beyond general stigma.
  • As many as 1 in 5 athletes experience mental health concerns, but few seek support despite high stress.
  • Asking for help is becoming part of what it means to be a strong athlete.
Source: Luke Stenson, Wyatt Porch, and Kendrick Stoddart, used with permission

College athletics demands a great deal from the people who compete: early mornings, relentless performance pressure, constant public evaluation, and the expectation that mental toughness is simply part of the job. For many student-athletes, asking for help feels like a direct contradiction of everything their sport has taught them to be.

Research consistently reveals a troubling gap. Despite high rates of anxiety, depression, and mental exhaustion among college athletes—one study estimated that as many as 1 in 5 experience some type of mental health concern—few seek formal mental health support.

To learn more about why student-athletes may resist seeking help, I spoke with Luke Stenson and Wyatt Porch, Division I athletes and co-creators of TheAthleteCheck, a mental health platform for student-athletes. They offer a firsthand look at what it feels like to navigate mental health inside a performance culture, and why that perspective matters.

When Identity Becomes a Barrier

For many student-athletes, the athletic role is not just something they do. It is who they are. Experts indicate that this kind of deep identification with sport can be a double-edged sword. Athletic identity can become a psychological liability when an athlete's sense of self depends almost entirely on performance. This risk is especially pronounced during injury, poor performance, or the transition out of sport entirely.

Research shows that stigma is one of the most significant barriers to help-seeking in athletic populations. Many athletes describe mental health struggles as fundamentally incompatible with being an athlete—a belief that performing at the highest level requires being mentally unbreakable. Stenson and Porch experienced this tension firsthand. "The barrier was never awareness," Porch noted. "Athletes know when they're struggling. The question is whether they believe asking for help is something athletes are allowed to do."

The Silence Underneath the Performance

Part of what makes this issue so difficult is that many student-athletes become skilled at pushing through distress and convincing themselves that nothing is wrong. Several studies have found that athletes often minimize their symptoms or believe mental health struggles are something that happens to other people, even when they are already experiencing them firsthand.

It is common for athletes to learn early on to push through pain, manage discomfort, and project confidence regardless of their internal state. These are genuinely useful skills in competition. In the context of mental health, however, they become obstacles. The same mental toughness that earns playing time can delay a conversation that would help.

Why the Solution Has to Come From Within

When athletic identity runs deep, support that comes from outside that world often does not register as credible.
Research shows that athletes frequently report low trust and discomfort when seeking help from providers outside their sport environment. When support comes from someone with no connection to athletic culture, it can feel removed from the pressures and realities student-athletes navigate every day. A study showed that peer support interventions with collegiate athletes significantly enhanced psychological resilience and reduced perceived stress, with relatability and shared experience identified as the key mechanisms driving those outcomes.

Stenson said, "We were the athletes who needed it. We knew what the real questions were—not the ones on a standard intake form." That inside perspective matters. When support comes from someone who has lived the same pressures, spoken the same language, and worn the same uniform, the conversation carries a credibility that outside intervention rarely can match.

Action Steps

Whether you are a student-athlete, coach, or someone who supports one, here are some practical steps to apply:

  1. Separate your identity from your performance: Your worth is not determined by your stats, playing time, or roster spot. Build a sense of self outside your sport—through relationships, interests, and values that exist regardless of how you perform.
  2. Check in with yourself the way you check your physical readiness: Before competition, most athletes assess their body. Ask yourself the same questions about your mental and emotional state: Am I carrying something into this that I have not dealt with? Is my head actually in this, or am I just going through the motions?
  3. Say something first: One honest conversation can change the entire feel of a locker room. Ask a teammate how they are really doing—and actually wait for the answer. Culture does not shift from a memo or a mandate. It shifts when one person decides to go first.
  4. Access support before you are in crisis: The athletes who benefit most from mental health resources are those who use them early. Waiting until you are overwhelmed makes everything harder, including asking for help.
  5. Start with someone who gets it: If professional support feels out of reach—or if you simply want an additional layer of support—find a teammate, former athlete, or someone in your sport who has been open about their own struggles and start there. That conversation is not a substitute for professional care, but for many athletes, it is what makes that call finally feel possible.

Bottom Line

Student-athletes are not struggling because they are weak. They are struggling because the culture that builds their strength also teaches them that asking for help is incompatible with who they are. But culture is not fixed. It shifts when the people inside it decide it should, and that shift is already happening, one honest conversation at a time.

© 2026 Ryan C. Warner, Ph.D.

item.title: Are You (Still) Beach Body Ready?
item.description:
Body Positivity

Are You (Still) Beach Body Ready?

What the pushback against an advertisement from a decade ago can teach us today.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Public backlash to the 2015 "beach body ready" advert marked a shift toward body positivity.
  • Social ideals of beauty have since intensified, with pressure to meet globalized, visual standards.
  • The outrage over beach body messaging might be less intense today, replaced by a resigned acceptance.

Co-authored by Heather Widdows and Jessica Sutherland, University of Warwick

It’s been over 10 years since Protein World’s notorious "beach body ready" advert received spontaneous pushback from the British public. The large yellow advert showed a beautiful blonde in a yellow bikini staring down the camera. It asked in large black letters, "Are you beach body ready?"

The emphatic response was—give us a break, sod that! In one way or another, people objected. The adverts on the London Underground—the metro—were routinely defaced. Sometimes, Protein World was told where to go; other times, the advert was answered, "Yes, you are." Pushbacks included "your body is fine just as it is" and "your body is not a commodity." When the campaign transferred to the U.S., it was greeted in the same way. The campaign went viral with the hashtag #eachbodysready. The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority received 378 complaints, and a change.org petition demanding the advert be removed amassed over 43,000 signatures.

Ultimately, the Advertising Standards Authority didn’t uphold the complaint, ruling that “the headline and image were unlikely to cause serious or widespread offence” and that they did “not consider the image of the model would shame women who had different body shapes into believing they needed to take a slimming supplement to feel confident wearing swimwear in public.”1 Despite doubling down and defending their advert, Protein World ended up pulling it over concerns that its health claims were not substantiated. The bottom line, no pun intended, is that it was ill-conceived, exactly the wrong message for the time.

But a decade on, things are different. In 2015, at the height of body positivity, #everybodysready wasn’t the only hashtag to go viral; others included #EffYourBeautyStandards, #CelebrateMySize, and #LoveYourBody. Over the decade, the pressure to be perfect has grown. Impossibly perfect glass skin is ideal, as are perfectly round peachy buttocks on slim legs, Barbie-esque snatched waists, and gravity-defying breasts. No longer are cosmetic procedures extreme, something done only by the rich or the vain; they are normal and normalised. Injectables are expected parts of beauty routines, necessary upkeep, with trips to the clinic as essential as trips to the hairdresser and dentist, and sometimes even done at the same time. And it seems like everyone is using GPL-1s as the tyranny of thinness bites like never before.

If many of us were asked today, "Are you beach body ready?" the answer would almost certainly be "no." Very likely, the "no" would be a resigned "no," with no shouting or defacing, an inevitable recognition that our bodies are far from perfect and we know it. How did we go from there to here? Part of the answer is the pandemic. Part is the move to a visual culture. And part of it is that the new ideal is global, normalising beauty practices and turning these practices into health and hygiene practices.

article continues after advertisement

But these are partial stories. Underlying all of this is a change in what we value, how we identify, and what we think appearance means. In a very real way, our bodies are now ourselves. We may value appearance more than ever before. Preteen girls are influencers teaching other preteen girls how to get perfect skin, even though their skin will never be more perfect. Women in their 20s are having preventive Botox, and men are feeling the pressure, too. The pressure to be beach body ready doesn’t seem as outrageous today as it did then. The world has changed.

item.title: The Power of Developing Executive Function
item.description:
Executive Function

The Power of Developing Executive Function

One student's transformation is a reminder of the impact of important skills.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Teaching our children executive function skills can positively change their lives.
  • All young people are developing executive functions as they grow.
  • Parents and teachers can support the development of skills like organizing, planning, and time management.

Myron sits across from me in the booth, his pancakes mostly untouched, his face smirking in reflection on his seventh-grade self. “I was such a mess back then,” he laughs. “I can’t believe you put up with me.” Myron’s in town to collaborate with fellow rental managers, called on to share his strategies for connecting tenants with community resources. His employer and the communities he serves celebrate his impact.

Seventh-grade Myron, however, was a different story. Devastated by a family death and struggling with undiagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Myron was that student on campus: the one all teachers knew but few had reached. His inner struggles were highly visible in his actions, words, and conflicts. When we met, he had, mostly accidentally, stepped on my foot on his way off the school bus, which was the same foot that had 17 surgeries. It was a painful start to what would be an incredible journey together.

“Did you see my Facebook post a few days ago?” he asks while we eat breakfast. He hands me his phone, and tears well up in my eyes at the photo of us: me in my favorite first-day-of-school dress and him with his backpack looking heavier than him. “It all started with a binder party,” his post begins, “and it was the first time I learned that I could learn how to learn and do school.”

A messy binder can indicate executive function needs.
Source: Willfried Wende/Pexels

Myron’s post celebrated a turning point that, at the time, felt like just another Thursday when we organized his backpack together. I got him a snack, he chose some music, and we dumped the contents of his backpack onto a table. While we explored his understanding of organization, we tested out systems that might work for his brain. We talked about school, home, and the waves of self-doubt that left him feeling defensive.

“What do you think was important about that time?” I ask him.

He ponders for a moment. “I don’t think I realized that there were options for me, that I could learn ways to do things that were hard for me. I thought everyone else was good at school, and I never would be. Everyone told me to try harder, but you taught me how to do the things. Sometimes, it was like we could hack school together.”

“Hacking” school began when Myron learned about and grew his executive function skills, which are the broad spectrum of mental actions people take to reach goals. When we empower our students, children, and teens to grow their executive function, their school and life experiences change tremendously. Our kids slowly emerge from the fixed mindset of areas like school or chores being terminally hard for them, and they begin to realize their potential for academic and executive function success.

Whether diagnosed with a learning difference or just growing up as an adolescent, inside each young person is a Myron, who may feel lost, defeated, or confused about how to do well in school. While school requires layers of specific skills, such as organizing and planning, our busy schedules at home and at school may not allow time to teach these requisite skills or, better yet, teach students how to identify their own needs and find resources to grow their skills. We may lament that students turn in their work late or don’t seem to focus in class, and yet we may also feel lost about how to address these challenges. It’s not like we can hit pause and teach How to Be a Student 101. How would we even teach these executive function skills?

Developing students’ executive function skills can take time (albeit not a lot of sweeping changes to your parenting or teaching). It often requires you to think about your own brain, learning, and the systems you use to facilitate your life. It will feel overwhelming at times. Yet, it may prove to be one of the most important shifts of your parenting or teaching experience.

As with many of the challenging journeys we undertake, developing our kids’ executive function skills is rewarding. It’s a positive snowball, a shot of espresso, an alive time in your home or classroom that begins as a hum and ends as a roar. Stick with yourself and your child during your journey, and the results will amaze you.

Adapted from Growing Executive Function, by Sarah Kesty, Copyright 2026.

item.title: When Scrolling Becomes a Problem
item.description:
Social Media

When Scrolling Becomes a Problem

What research and the law tell us about teens and social media.

Posted June 30, 2026

Key points
  • Research documents the health consequences of problematic social media use, especially for teens.
  • As teens are growing and developing, they are especially vulnerable to addictive behaviors.
  • The evidence shows that strong guidance from parents, therapy, and education can help.
Source: Antto-AI/Adobe Stock

In a landmark decision earlier this year, a California jury found Meta and Google liable for designing social media platforms (namely Instagram and YouTube) that harmed the mental health of a young woman. The jury concluded the companies acted with malice by engineering features to promote compulsive behavior, which led to symptoms of anxiety, body dysmorphia, and depression for the plaintiff. They awarded her $6 million in damages.

The verdict sets a new legal precedent, but for researchers who study adolescent social media use, the findings were familiar. A growing body of evidence documents the health risks of social media addiction among youth.

The word "addiction" is often used loosely, and, in fact, social media addiction is not recognized as an official disorder in the DSM. But researchers have applied clinical frameworks to measure social media addiction, and a series of studies have found evidence of this growing problem in teens across the globe. In a nationally representative survey of adolescent girls in the U.S., more than one-third reported feeling “addicted” to a social media platform. In another survey, more than 35 percent of U.S. teens reported using at least one social media platform “almost constantly.” A study of teenagers in Pakistan found that about 12 percent exhibit signs of social media addiction. And a study of over 1,000 Turkish adolescents found that 23 percent met criteria for social media addiction.

Research shows that teens are especially vulnerable to problematic social media use because of the unique interplay between the developing brain and the design of social media platforms. During adolescence, young people are forming their identities and learning how to communicate with others. When they interact on social media, they only see the curated identities of their peers, which is likely to heighten feelings of inferiority, which often leads teens to engage even more with social media.

The same study shows how the features of social media platforms drive addiction. For example, platforms with the infinite scroll feature allow users to explore content constantly without interruptions, making it easy to lose track of time. Social comparison and seeking validation through likes and comments also lead to increased time spent on social media platforms.

The Mental Health Toll

The effects of social media addiction on teen mental health are well-documented. A large systematic review found that it leads to depression and lower academic performance, a diminished sense of well-being, and lower quality social relationships. Other research links social media addiction to anxiety, depression, and emotional distress.

Another recent study found that for many teens, social media addiction mirrors addiction to other substances, with symptoms including withdrawal and impaired functioning. In the study, researchers asked 11- and 12-year-olds to respond to statements about reducing their social media use and their feelings when they can’t use it. About 16 percent of participants said they tried to use social media less, but couldn’t, and 23 percent said they spent a lot of time thinking about their social media apps.

What Actually Helps

Research is also helping us to understand the best interventions to counteract social media addiction. So far, here’s what we know works:

  • Cognitive behavioral therapy can help teens change unhealthy thought patterns and behaviors and make more conscious choices about social media use.
  • The evidence shows that parental supervision and strong, loving relationships with parents are protective against social media addiction. Setting clear boundaries around device use—especially at night and during meals—and having open, nonjudgmental conversations about what teens are experiencing online are effective ways to prevent problematic social media use.
  • Mindfulness-based approaches can help teens develop awareness of their own usage patterns and emotional triggers, building the self-regulation skills that addiction undermines.
  • Educating teens about social media addiction allows them to recognize the risks and consequences of excessive social media use. Presentations at schools, workshops, and online resources can motivate teens to think about and discuss their struggles and destigmatize social media dependence.

The take-home message: Problematic social media use is currently a real problem with negative impacts on adolescent mental health. For parents navigating this issue, the evidence shows that interventions work, including setting boundaries for social media use, maintaining a close relationship with your teen, prioritizing education about social media addiction, and turning to therapy if problems arise.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
